data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism is self-undermining: it claims the preference is rational because the best-corroborated theory 'is the most efficient vehicle for further testing' and 'maximizes the chance of quickly falsifying a false theory,' but this very claim requires an inductive bridge from past testing performance to future testing efficiency. If corroboration is merely 'a report of past performance' carrying no future probability (as the target insists), then there is no non-inductive basis for asserting that a theory which survived severe tests yesterday will be an efficient vehicle for testing today. The mechanism thus smuggles in the assumption that past testing history is informative about future falsification speed — the very inductive assumption the target purports to renounce. The target's own countercondition 3 identifies this collapse, but the mechanism does not actually avoid it; it merely relabels the inductive inference ('likely true') as a different inductive inference ('likely efficient for testing').
